name: Pontianak
origin: Kalimantan-Malay form of the Kuntilanak complex; the city of Pontianak is said to be named for her. Woman who died in childbirth, haunting banyan and banana trees.
behavior: Long white dress, long black hair, sweet frangipani scent turning foul; attacks men, targets pregnant women.
deterrents: Nail driven into the hole at the nape of her neck is said to tame her into a wife.
popCulture: Namesake of the West Kalimantan capital; frequent film subject.

name: Kuntilanak Merah
origin: Red-clad, more aggressive urban variant of the Kuntilanak reported from the 2000s onward.
behavior: Red dress instead of white; laughter said to be louder and closer than it sounds.
deterrents: As for Kuntilanak: iron, prayers, avoiding her trees at night.
popCulture: Viral-era urban legend and film variant.

name: Nyai Blorong
origin: Serpent queen of the pesugihan world, half woman half snake, who grants wealth in gold that turns to leaves or demands a price.
appearance: Beautiful woman above, golden-scaled serpent below; palace beneath the sea or in caves.
behavior: Enter pesugihan pacts through offerings; wealth is illusory or short-lived.
deterrents: Breaking the pact; religious devotion.
popCulture: Major figure in Javanese occult lore and sinetron.

name: Dewi Lanjar
origin: Queen of the north coast sea around Pekalongan, junior counterpart to Nyi Roro Kidul of the south coast; guardian of fishermen and gamblers' luck.
appearance: Regal woman in green-gold dress appearing near the northern shore.
behavior: Grants luck and protection to fishermen who honour her; punishes greed.
deterrents: Offerings and humility; she withdraws favor from the arrogant.
popCulture: Central to Pekalongan coastal folklore.

name: Nyi Pelet
origin: Legendary witch of the Mount Kemukus / Jampang tradition, master of pelet love magic that binds victims' will.
appearance: Appears as a beautiful woman; her power works at a distance through spells and effigies.
behavior: Causes obsessive, ruinous love in targets chosen by clients.
deterrents: Counter-magic by a stronger dukun; religious protection.
popCulture: Her name is now generic Indonesian slang for love magic.

name: Calon Arang
origin: Historical-legendary widow-witch of Girah (12th c. Daha kingdom) whose plague magic forced a royal marriage alliance; her book of magic stolen by Bahula in the tale.
appearance: Terrifying crone with wild hair and long tongue in Balinese tellings and dance.
behavior: Unleashes plague and pestilence on villages that insult her daughter.
deterrents: Her own spellbook turned against her; in the tale, death at her master's word.
popCulture: Subject of Balinese Calonarang dance-drama still performed today.

name: Kolor Ijo
origin: 2000s urban-panic demon in green underpants blamed for attacks on women in Java; part moral panic, part folklore.
appearance: Muscular figure wearing only green underwear, superhumanly strong.
behavior: Breaks into homes at night; associated with black-magic empowerment.
deterrents: Communal patrols (ronda) and prayers; several human suspects were arrested in the panics.
popCulture: A modern, media-age Indonesian folk demon.

name: Pastur Kepala Buntung
origin: Headless Dutch-era priest said to walk Jakarta cemeteries (notably Jeruk Purut) carrying his own head.
appearance: Black priestly robes, head carried under one arm, sometimes with a large black dog.
behavior: Wanders at night; seeing him is an omen rather than a direct attack in most tellings.
deterrents: None specific; he is avoided rather than fought.
popCulture: One of Jakarta's most retold cemetery legends.

name: Hantu Jeruk Purut
origin: The collective haunting of Jeruk Purut cemetery, South Jakarta, anchored by the headless priest and a child spirit with a black dog.
appearance: Shifting apparitions among the graves after dark.
behavior: Manifests to night visitors and film crews; largely place-bound.
deterrents: Respectful conduct in the cemetery.
popCulture: Subject of the 2006 film Hantu Jeruk Purut.

name: Kereta Hantu Manggarai
origin: Ghost train said to run the Manggarai line in Jakarta without a driver, linked in legend to the 1987 Bintaro crash.
appearance: An old train passing at night with dark or empty carriages.
behavior: Appears on the tracks after midnight; hearing it is a death omen in some versions.
deterrents: None; a place-and-time-bound urban legend.
popCulture: Staple of Indonesian urban-legend media.

name: Hantu Ambulans Bandung
origin: Bandung urban legend of an ambulance endlessly repeating its last fatal journey from a house on Jalan Bahureksa.
appearance: An old ambulance with siren and a patient or nurse visible inside.
behavior: Circles the same route at night; the house's doorbell rings by itself in the legend.
deterrents: None specific.
popCulture: Subject of a 2008 horror film of the same name.

name: Mak Lampir
origin: Cackling witch of Mount Merapi from the long-running Misteri Gunung Merapi radio/TV serial, absorbed into popular folklore.
appearance: Green-faced crone with wild hair, clawed hands and a screeching laugh.
behavior: Schemes for power and revenge from her mountain lair.
deterrents: Heroes' magic and her own overreach.
popCulture: One of Indonesia's most recognisable TV horror villains (1980s-2000s).

name: Grandong
origin: Betawi pesugihan beast kept for wealth and guarding property, demanding food offerings and eventually a human price.
appearance: Dog- or ape-like black beast with glowing eyes.
behavior: Guards the keeper's house; steals and intimidates neighbours.
deterrents: The pact's terms turning on the keeper; religious cleansing.
popCulture: Recurring figure in Betawi occult tales.

name: Pocong Merah
origin: Red-shrouded, angry variant of the Pocong from urban reports; the red shroud signals a violent or unavenged death.
appearance: Pocong form with a blood-red shroud and darkened face.
behavior: More mobile and aggressive than the white Pocong; chases witnesses.
deterrents: Untying the shroud knot; prayers for the dead.
popCulture: Urban-legend and viral-video variant.

name: Orang Bunian
origin: The 'hidden people' of Malay and Sumatran forests: an invisible parallel society whose villages, music and weddings mortals sometimes glimpse or enter.
appearance: Perfectly human-like but hollow-backed or otherwise subtly wrong; fine clothes.
behavior: Invite or abduct mortals; time inside Bunian villages runs differently, returnees age years in a night.
deterrents: Iron, prayers, and refusing Bunian food.
popCulture: Across the Malay world; comparable to European fairy abduction lore.

name: Hantu Galah
origin: Long-limbed tree ghost of the Malay world whose arms and legs stretch like poles (galah) among canopy branches.
appearance: Impossibly tall, thin figure looming between trees.
behavior: Reaches down at forest travelers; mostly a terror of deep forest.
deterrents: Avoiding its groves at dusk.
popCulture: Widespread Malay forest lore.

name: Hantu Tinggi
origin: The 'tall ghost' of Malay tradition: the longer you look up at it, the taller it grows, until it towers over the trees.
appearance: Humanoid of escalating height, face often unseen.
behavior: Grows with the victim's gaze; associated with rubber estates and forest edges.
deterrents: Look away and run; do not meet its gaze.
popCulture: Close relative of Begu Ganjang in neighbouring Batak lore.

name: Hantu Kopek
origin: Malay old-woman ghost named for her long, hanging breasts, said to hide children or lead them astray near villages.
appearance: stooped crone with exaggerated hanging breasts.
behavior: Hides kidnapped children (echoing Wewe Gombel) and frightens night travelers.
deterrents: Calling the child's name; iron and prayers.
popCulture: Documented in Malay ghost catalogues since colonial era.

name: Hantu Rimba
origin: Generic but named class of deep-jungle spirits in Malay lore, owners of game and places hunters must placate.
appearance: Rarely seen directly; signs are sounds, smells and sudden silence.
behavior: Misleads hunters, hides game or paths from the disrespectful.
deterrents: Offerings and forest etiquette (asking permission).
popCulture: Part of living Malay hunting tradition.

name: Mambang
origin: Class of Malay nature spirits tied to specific phenomena — Mambang Putih (daylight), Kuning (dusk), and others color-coded by time and element.
appearance: Coloured radiance or presence rather than a body.
behavior: Influence weather, mood and fortune of a place.
deterrents: Ritual courtesy; shamans (pawang) negotiate with them.
popCulture: Codified in classic Malay magical texts.

name: Putri Tangguk
origin: Jambi legend of a woman who wasted rice while husking and was cursed to repeat her labour forever; a cautionary spirit of waste.
appearance: Woman endlessly pounding rice at night near fields and granaries.
behavior: Her pounding is heard at night; she embodies punishment for wasting food.
deterrents: Respect for rice; finishing one's food.
popCulture: A moral-ecological legend still told to children in Jambi.

name: Mariaban
origin: Dayak hairy giant of Kalimantan forests, a large red-haired wild man distinct from Orang Pendek by size.
appearance: Two-metre hairy biped with long arms.
behavior: Avoids humans; blamed for crop raids and forest noises.
deterrents: None needed; treated as a biological entity in local accounts.
popCulture: Kalimantan counterpart in the SE Asian wild-man complex.

name: Hantu Banyu
origin: Banjar water ghost (banyu = water) haunting South Kalimantan rivers, pulling swimmers and boatmen under.
appearance: Formless presence or pale figure in the current.
behavior: Drownings at known haunted stretches of river.
deterrents: River offerings; avoiding named spots at dusk.
popCulture: Living river lore among Banjar communities.

name: Anak Sima
origin: Kept spirit-child of Kalimantan occult practice, fed milk and blood, bringing luck and theft to its keeper.
appearance: Small child figure, sometimes only heard crying.
behavior: Steals small goods and money for its keeper; demands constant feeding.
deterrents: Neglect turns it on the keeper; disposal requires a specialist.
popCulture: Regional cognate of the Tuyul complex.

name: Hantu Buaya Putih
origin: White crocodile as ancestral guardian or transformed human (jadi-jadian) in Kalimantan and wider Malay river lore.
appearance: Albino crocodile of unusual size and intelligence.
behavior: Guards river stretches and treasure; attacks the greedy or taboo-breaking.
deterrents: Taboo observance; it is protected, not fought, in most tellings.
popCulture: White crocodiles are still treated as sacred at several Indonesian rivers.

name: Memedi
origin: Balinese playful child ghost — the everyday word memedi means a spook used to scare children; in lore a mischievous small spirit.
appearance: Small shadowy child figure at the edge of yards and fields.
behavior: Plays tricks, hides objects, laughs from rooftops.
deterrents: Mostly harmless; offerings of sweets.
popCulture: Everyday Balinese household folklore.

name: Tonya
origin: Balinese river and spring guardians (tonya) inhabiting water sources, receiving offerings at temples like Tirta Gangga's springs.
appearance: Unseen presence at springs, occasionally a figure in the water.
behavior: Guard water quality and quantity; punish pollution and theft of water.
deterrents: Offerings and keeping springs clean — a living conservation ethic.
popCulture: Tonya shrines remain active at Balinese springs.

name: Naga Besukih
origin: The great dragon of Mount Agung whose tail is said to reach the sea; his shifting causes tremors in Balinese cosmology.
appearance: Vast serpent coiled inside the volcano.
behavior: His movements explain earthquakes; he anchors the island's cosmic order.
deterrents: Temple offerings at Besakih, on Agung's slopes.
popCulture: Central to the Besakih temple complex mythology.

name: Parakang
origin: Bugis-Makassar flying-head feeder, often treated as the local name/form of the Poppo complex — kept as a separate taxon here, synonymy debated.
appearance: Head with trailing entrails flying at night, by day a normal person.
behavior: Attacks pregnant women, infants and the sick; the transformation is hereditary or learned.
deterrents: Thorns and sharp leaves under the house; vinegar on the neck stump.
popCulture: One of South Sulawesi's most feared beings.

name: Pokpok
origin: Sulawesi flying feeder identified by its 'pok-pok' call — the louder the call, the farther away it is said to be (inverse of natural sound).
appearance: Rarely seen; defined by its call and night flights.
behavior: Hunts like the Parakang complex it belongs to.
deterrents: As for Parakang.
popCulture: A nice case of a taxon diagnosed by a behavioural character alone.

name: Longga
origin: Bugis tall ghost whose head reaches the coconut palms; kin to Hantu Tinggi and Begu Ganjang.
appearance: Towering thin figure among palm crowns.
behavior: Terrifies by scale alone; appears at field edges at dusk.
deterrents: Averting the gaze; leaving its ground.
popCulture: Part of the pan-archipelago 'tall ghost' character complex.

name: Waruga Spirit
origin: Ancestral spirits housed in waruga, the carved stone tombs of the Minahasa, guarding descendants and clan land.
appearance: Presence at stone sarcophagi carved with the ancestor's life.
behavior: Guardianship and blessing; anger at tomb desecration.
deterrents: Offerings and tomb care.
popCulture: Waruga sites (e.g. Airmadidi) are protected heritage today.

name: Jin Qarin
origin: In Islamic teaching as practised in Indonesia, every person has a qarin — a jinn companion who whispers temptation and may linger or be seen after death, explaining many 'ghost' sightings.
appearance: Identical double of its person.
behavior: Tempts and misleads; post-mortem sightings attributed to it.
deterrents: Prayer, Qur'an recitation (ruqyah).
popCulture: Explains a large share of Indonesian haunting reports in religious framing.

name: Preta
origin: The preta of Hindu-Buddhist cosmology retained in Bali and Javanese tradition: the greedy dead reborn with huge bellies and needle throats, never able to eat.
appearance: Emaciated figure with swollen belly and tiny mouth.
behavior: Wanders in torment; fed by offerings (e.g. during Pitra Paksha / Galungan cycles).
deterrents: Merit-making and food offerings by descendants.
popCulture: The archipelago's link to the pan-Asian hungry-ghost complex.

name: Hantu Air
origin: Generic name for drowning water ghosts across the archipelago — the spirit of a drowned person or a place-spirit that claims a victim, often said to need a replacement.
appearance: Pale figure or grip from below the surface at rivers, wells and lakes.
behavior: Pulls swimmers down; haunted waters are said to take a victim periodically.
deterrents: Offerings; avoiding named waters at dusk; not swimming alone.
popCulture: A functional category uniting many local river ghosts.

name: Dedemit
origin: Javanese land and place demons — the wild counterpart to village guardians, owners of forests, crossroads and empty land.
appearance: Seldom fully seen; a heavy presence, smell or partial figure.
behavior: Punishes trespass and building without permission.
deterrents: Permission rituals (permisi) and offerings before clearing land.
popCulture: Still invoked in Javanese land-clearing etiquette.

name: Lelembut
origin: The 'refined ones' — Javanese invisible beings of higher, subtler order than dedemit, including ancestral and place spirits in kejawen cosmology.
appearance: Invisible or seen in meditation and dreams.
behavior: Possession (kesurupan) and guidance through mediums.
deterrents: Ritual specialists mediate contact.
popCulture: Core concept of Javanese spiritual taxonomy.

name: Peri
origin: Peri of Malay tales: beautiful winged female nature spirits of forests and mountains, from Persian pari via Malay literature.
appearance: Small radiant winged woman.
behavior: Mostly benevolent; aids heroes, guards wild places.
deterrents: Courtesy; iron is harmful to her kind in some tales.
popCulture: Staple of hikayat literature and Malay pantun.

name: Jin Tanah
origin: Earth jinn of Malay magic, bound to soil and foundations; disturbed by digging and construction, appeased in groundbreaking rites.
appearance: Unseen; signs are illness and accidents on site.
behavior: Causes mishaps when its ground is broken without rite.
deterrents: Groundbreaking offerings led by a pawang.
popCulture: Rites for jin tanah persist in Malay building custom.

name: Orang Minyak
origin: The 'oily man' of Malay lore: a black-magic practitioner (or transformed being) coated in oil, impossible to grip, who attacks women at night; waves of sightings hit Malaysia and Sumatra repeatedly from the 1950s on.
appearance: Naked human figure glistening with black oil.
behavior: Slips all grasps; empowered by a rape-count pact in the darkest versions.
deterrents: Flour or ash to break the oil's slipperiness in folk advice.
popCulture: Subject of classic Malay films (1958) and periodic modern panics.

name: Jerangkung
origin: Javanese kept spirit housed in a small skeleton-like effigy, fed and questioned like an oracle, kin to the Jenglot complex.
appearance: Miniature skeleton figure kept in a box or shrine.
behavior: Answers questions, guards property and steals for its keeper.
deterrents: Starving or ritually disposing of the effigy.
popCulture: Part of the Indonesian kept-object (pusaka hidup) tradition.

name: Siluman Ular
origin: Siluman ular — snake-beings that take human form, marry mortals in folktales, and guard treasure or graves across the archipelago.
appearance: Beautiful human with snake traits (forked habits, shed skin found nearby).
behavior: Marriage and treasure-guarding tales; dangerous if its skin is stolen or burned.
deterrents: Returning or burning the shed skin in variant tales.
popCulture: A whole tale-type (ATU-like) across Indonesian folktale collections.

name: Roh Komodo
origin: On Komodo and Rinca, dragons are kin: the legend of the Dragon Princess who bore twins, one human one dragon, makes the ora (Komodo dragon) an ancestral sibling, not a monster.
appearance: The living dragon itself as ancestor.
behavior: Protecting dragons is protecting family; attacks read as broken kinship.
deterrents: Kinship taboos — dragons are not killed on the islands.
popCulture: Basis of Komodo Islanders' conservation relationship with the dragons.

name: Hantu Yauw
origin: Yauw-type malevolent bush spirits of Papuan highland lore, blamed for illness and misfortune away from the village.
appearance: Seldom seen; illness and night sounds are its signs.
behavior: Afflicts travelers and gardens at the forest edge.
deterrents: Healing and protective rites by elders.
popCulture: Recorded in ethnographies of highlands Papua.

name: Penunggu
origin: The penunggu — 'the one who waits/keeps' — guardian spirit of a house, tree, bridge, school or office; the single most common category in everyday Indonesian haunting reports.
appearance: Manifests as the place requires: a figure, a smell, a presence, a dream warning.
behavior: Guards its place; objects to renovation, felling or disrespect; school and office hauntings are usually penunggu.
deterrents: Offerings and permission before altering the place.
popCulture: The default explanation in contemporary Indonesian ghost talk.

name: Aswang
origin: Philippine umbrella feeder that splits, flies, or transforms to eat viscera, fetuses and corpses — the closest regional comparator to the whole Indonesian flying-head complex.
appearance: Variable: woman, animal, or flying torso by region.
behavior: Nocturnal predation on pregnant women, children and the dead.
deterrents: Garlic, salt, ash, stingray-tail whips.
popCulture: Outgroup: defines the wider SE Asian viscerophage radiation.

name: Tikbalang
origin: Philippine horse-headed humanoid that misleads travelers into walking in circles in forests and bamboo groves.
appearance: Tall figure with a horse's head and long limbs.
behavior: Reverses travelers' sense of direction; associated with storms and big trees.
deterrents: Wearing one's shirt inside-out breaks its trick.
popCulture: Outgroup comparator for Indonesian therianthropes.

name: Phi Tai Hong
origin: Thai ghost of a person who died violently or suddenly — among the most feared in Thai taxonomy, lingering at the death site for a set period.
appearance: As in life, often showing the fatal injury.
behavior: Haunts aggressively; especially dangerous in the first days after death.
deterrents: Merit-making and monk-led rites to release it.
popCulture: Outgroup comparator for the vengeful-death complex.

name: Churel
origin: South Asian ghost of a woman who died in childbirth or by injustice, with backward feet and a taste for young men's life force — the deep outgroup showing how far the vengeful-mother complex extends.
appearance: Beautiful woman from the front; feet point backward.
behavior: Seduces and drains young men; haunts crossroads and childbirth places.
deterrents: Burial face-down with thorns and iron in classic accounts.
popCulture: Outgroup: root comparator west of SE Asia.

name: Jembalang
origin: Malay earth demon of wild places, the untamed counterpart invoked when land is cleared; a jembalang tanah must be propitiated before any digging or building.
appearance: Rarely seen whole; a hulking presence, animal shapes, or a figure at the treeline.
behavior: Attacks or sickens those who clear land, dig wells or build without permission.
deterrents: Permission rites and offerings led by a pawang before work begins.
popCulture: One of the classic categories in Skeat's Malay Magic (1900).

name: Hantu Raya
origin: The 'great ghost' of Malay sorcery: a powerful familiar bound to a master, fed on offerings, growing stronger than its keeper over time.
appearance: Appears in the master's shape or as a huge dark figure.
behavior: Does its master's bidding — theft, harm, guarding — and demands escalating offerings.
deterrents: A stronger bomoh must bind or destroy it; it turns on a neglectful keeper.
popCulture: Benchmark familiar of Malay magical lore.

name: Pelesit
origin: Malay female-associated familiar spirit kept in a bottle, taking grasshopper form, paired with the Polong; said to be inherited or made from a dead child's tongue in classic accounts.
appearance: A grasshopper, or a tiny woman's head with a sharp proboscis.
behavior: Attacks victims chosen by its mistress, causing madness and wasting; cries betray its presence.
deterrents: Burial of the bottle, exorcism by a bomoh.
popCulture: Documented since colonial-era Malay magic texts.

name: Polong
origin: Malay familiar created and kept in a bottle (polong = the vessel-spirit), fed blood from its owner's finger, sent to possess and waste enemies.
appearance: A small fiery or smoky figure slipping from its bottle.
behavior: Possesses victims, who rave and reveal the sender's name under exorcism.
deterrents: Exorcism forces it to name its owner; destroying the bottle ends it.
popCulture: The Pelesit-Polong pair is the classic Malay familiar complex.

name: Datuk Keramat
origin: Venerated guardian spirits of place in the Malay world — deified ancestors, saints or local heroes enshrined at keramat graves and trees, worshipped across Malay, Chinese and Indian communities.
appearance: Shrines rather than apparitions: graves, termite mounds, old trees with offerings.
behavior: Protects its place and grants help; punishes disrespect of the shrine.
deterrents: Offerings and respect; a protector, not an enemy.
popCulture: Keramat shrines dot Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula to this day.

name: Hantu Laut
origin: Sea ghost of Malay fishermen, master of dangerous waters, addressed in the Ulek Mayang healing ritual tradition for those struck down at sea.
appearance: A presence in waves and wind; the ritual summons it as a sea princess's retinue.
behavior: Claims fishermen and causes trance-illness in those it desires.
deterrents: The Ulek Mayang ritual negotiates the victim's soul back.
popCulture: Ulek Mayang is now a signature Terengganu-Malay performance.

name: Hantu Keramat
origin: Guardian of keramat — sacred graves, wells and groves — distinct from the deified Datuk by being the place's own wild keeper.
appearance: A white figure or animal (often a tiger) at the sacred site.
behavior: Strikes the sacrilegious with illness or misfortune.
deterrents: Offerings and asking permission (minta izin).
popCulture: Everyday protective geography across the Malay world.

name: Putri Gunung Ledang
origin: The fairy princess of Mount Ledang (Johor) who set Sultan Mahmud of Melaka seven impossible conditions — including a bowl of his son's blood — in the Sejarah Melayu; the Malay world's great refusal legend.
appearance: A radiantly beautiful princess attended by fairy maidens on the summit.
behavior: Tests suitors with impossible demands; guards the mountain still.
deterrents: None; she is sovereign, not fought.
popCulture: Subject of the 2004 film Puteri Gunung Ledang.

name: Setan Gundul
origin: Bald-headed demon of modern Javanese urban lore, a small shaved-headed figure blamed for disturbances and viral 'sightings' in the social-media era.
appearance: Small bald child-like figure, often photographed as a blur.
behavior: Appears in homes, roadsides and CCTV-era anecdotes.
deterrents: Prayers and house cleansing.
popCulture: A meme-age folk demon, spread by phone cameras.

name: Jailangkung
morphology: Invited spirit in a doll vessel
origin: Indonesia's famous spirit-summoning game: a spirit is invited into a basket-and-coconut doll with a pencil, and answers questions by moving it — 'datang tak dijemput, pulang tak diantar' (comes uninvited if not sent home properly).
appearance: A dressed basket doll with coconut-shell head.
behavior: Answers questions; the danger is a spirit that refuses to leave.
deterrents: The closing rite must send the spirit away; neglecting it invites a haunting.
popCulture: Subject of hit films Jelangkung (2001) onward, which revived the game nationwide.

name: Nini Thowok
origin: Javanese doll-spirit rite, female counterpart of Jailangkung: a spirit called into a coconut-and-basket doll, traditionally by women, once used in drought-time rain calling and village divination.
appearance: A doll dressed as an old woman (nini = grandmother).
behavior: Dances and answers while held by two handlers in trance play.
deterrents: Proper dismissal rite.
popCulture: Classic Javanese folk-game scholarship subject.

name: Hantu Terowongan Casablanca
origin: The woman of the Casablanca tunnel underpass in Jakarta, said to have died there after an assault in local legend; drivers report a figure crossing before their cars at night.
appearance: Woman in white or red standing in the tunnel or suddenly in the road.
behavior: Appears to drivers; swerving to avoid her is blamed for accidents.
deterrents: None specific; a place-bound urban haunting.
popCulture: Among Jakarta's most repeated road-ghost legends.

name: Hantu Rumah Kentang
origin: The 'Potato House' of Dharmawangsa, South Jakarta: legend of a child who died in a pot of boiling potatoes, whose crying and the smell of potatoes haunt the empty house.
appearance: A child's crying and the smell of boiled potatoes; the child is rarely seen.
behavior: Audible and olfactory haunting of one famous address.
deterrents: None; the house stood empty for decades on the legend's strength.
popCulture: Subject of the 2012 film Rumah Kentang.

name: Hantu Rumah Darmo
origin: Surabaya's Rumah Hantu Darmo: a pesugihan-ruined family's mansion, abandoned after the family died at sea when their wealth-pact came due, in the city's defining haunted-house legend.
appearance: Figures in the windows of a derelict luxury house; sounds of a family that is not there.
behavior: The house itself is the phenomenon — visitors report pressure, voices, apparitions.
deterrents: None; a cautionary pesugihan tale made architectural.
popCulture: East Java's most famous haunted house, a staple of local TV expeditions.

name: Hantu Lawang Sewu
origin: Lawang Sewu, the 'thousand doors' former Dutch railway headquarters in Semarang, is haunted in legend by Dutch ladies and by victims of its basement's wartime use as a prison.
appearance: A Dutch woman in period dress on the stairs and in the B building.
behavior: Place-bound apparitions; among Indonesia's most visited 'haunted' heritage sites.
deterrents: None; the site is now a museum managing its own legend.
popCulture: A fixture of Indonesian haunted-place rankings.

name: Seblang
origin: The Seblang of Banyuwangi: an ancestral spirit that possesses a chosen dancer (traditionally an older woman in Olehsari, a young one in Bakungan) for days of trance dance to cleanse the village — a living ritual, not a horror figure.
appearance: The possessed dancer in banana-leaf crown, dancing with closed eyes for hours or days.
behavior: Possession is invited and communal; the spirit blesses crops and the village.
deterrents: The ritual itself is the management: gamelan, handlers, offerings.
popCulture: One of Indonesia's best-documented living possession rituals.

name: Eyang Jugo
origin: Guardian ancestor of the Gunung Kawi tomb complex in Malang regency, East Java — the archipelago's most famous pesugihan pilgrimage site, where seekers meditate for wealth blessings at the tombs of Eyang Jugo and Raden Mas Iman Soedjono.
appearance: Enshrined tombs rather than apparitions; dreams and signs are his medium.
behavior: Grants or withholds the site's blessings; the ritual economy around him is the phenomenon.
deterrents: Offerings, meditation vigils, ritual etiquette.
popCulture: Gunung Kawi pilgrimage draws thousands each Jumat Legi night.

name: Arwah Penasaran
origin: The penasaran: the everyday Indonesian category for a soul that died with unfinished business or curiosity (penasaran = lingering curiosity) and so cannot move on — the default diagnosis for most hauntings.
appearance: As in life, often at the place of death.
behavior: Repeats its death circumstances, seeks help or acknowledgment.
deterrents: Prayers for the dead (tahlilan), finishing its business, religious rites.
popCulture: The concept organises ordinary Indonesian ghost talk more than any named species.

name: Bhuta Kala
origin: Bhuta Kala: the class of raw, disruptive nature forces in Balinese Hinduism — not fought but fed and harmonised (bhuta yadnya), most visibly in the Tawur Kesanga offerings before Nyepi when ogoh-ogoh effigies parade them through the streets.
appearance: Effigies (ogoh-ogoh) of fanged giants burned or paraded at year's end.
behavior: Disruption when out of balance; order when honoured.
deterrents: Offerings (caru) restore balance; exorcism misses the point — it is management, not war.
popCulture: Ogoh-ogoh parades are Bali's most spectacular public ritual art.

name: Barong Landung
origin: Barong Landung: the towering black male (Jero Gedé) and white female (Jero Luh) effigy pair, plague-era guardians processed village to village in Bali to expel epidemic disease.
appearance: Giant puppets three to four metres tall, male black-faced, female white-faced.
behavior: Paraded to absorb and carry away sickness and misfortune.
deterrents: They are the remedy, not the threat.
popCulture: Still processed in parts of Bali, notably around Sanur and during outbreaks.

name: Wong Samar
origin: The wong samar, Bali's 'dim/indistinct people': an invisible society paralleling humans, whose villages overlap ours and into which people occasionally vanish — Bali's cognate of Orang Bunian.
appearance: Human-like but unseen except at glimpses, markets at odd hours, or in dreams.
behavior: Abduction-by-hospitality: mortals entertained in samar villages lose track of years.
deterrents: Iron, prayers, refusing their food.
popCulture: Core of Balinese everyday spirit geography.

name: Gamang
origin: Gamang: the general Balinese class of subtle spirit beings inhabiting places, objects and crossroads, propitiated with daily canang offerings — the background population of Bali's spirit world.
appearance: Mostly invisible; small shrines (penunggun karang) mark their places in every house yard.
behavior: Influence household fortune; neglected gamang bring unease and illness.
deterrents: Daily offerings keep relations good.
popCulture: Every Balinese house yard shrine is gamang infrastructure.

name: Suster Keramas
origin: Denpasar urban legend of a nurse ghost whose hair-washing (keramas) is heard in a hospital bathroom; she is said to approach anyone who knocks or calls, asking to have her hair washed — with a handful of hair as the horror's price.
appearance: A nurse in old-fashioned uniform, wet-haired, face hidden.
behavior: Auditory haunting escalating to appearance in hospital retellings.
deterrents: None specific.
popCulture: Bali's best-known hospital ghost story.

name: Antu Nabau
origin: Nabau, the Iban giant serpent spirit of rivers and deep pools, large enough in omen accounts to swallow boats; a being of dreams and augury as much as of water.
appearance: A serpent of impossible size glimpsed in rivers or dreams.
behavior: Appears before great undertakings; both omen and predator.
deterrents: Ritual specialists read and answer its omens.
popCulture: Central figure in Iban augural tradition.

name: Antu Gerasi
origin: Antu Gerasi, the Iban huntsman spirit — a spectral hunter whose success in the spirit world mirrors and enables human hunting and, historically, headhunting raids.
appearance: A hunter figure with dogs, heard baying in the forest at night.
behavior: His hunts precede human ones; meeting him is a grave omen or a great blessing depending on rite.
deterrents: Offerings and augury before expeditions.
popCulture: Documented across Iban ethnography.

name: Hantu Sumiati
origin: Makassar's defining urban ghost: Sumiati, said in the legend to have hanged herself after a forced marriage or assault, haunting the city (notably around Jalan Gunung Merapi and the former Niaga area) since the 1990s retellings.
appearance: Woman in white or school uniform, sometimes on a becak at night.
behavior: Appears to becak drivers and night travelers; her story anchors Makassar ghost lore.
deterrents: None specific.
popCulture: Subject of the 2015 film Hantu Nancy / Sumiati cycle of South Sulawesi horror.

name: Kuang Waya
origin: Kuang Waya, malevolent spirit of Minahasa lore invoked in older accounts of illness and forest danger in North Sulawesi.
appearance: A dread presence in old-growth forest and graveyards.
behavior: Blamed for sickness and disappearance in traditional accounts.
deterrents: Christian and adat rites in modern tellings.
popCulture: Part of recorded Minahasan spirit taxonomy.

name: Opo Empung
origin: The opo: deified ancestors and place deities of traditional Minahasa religion (Alifuru), headed by Opo Empung, the supreme ancestor — the beings to whom waruga tombs and walian rituals were addressed.
appearance: Shrines, stones and ancestral places rather than apparitions.
behavior: Ancestral governance of land, harvest and conduct.
deterrents: Offerings and walian priestly ritual (historically).
popCulture: Foundation of pre-Christian Minahasa cosmology.

name: Polahi
origin: The Polahi of Gorontalo: 'those who fled' — communities said to have escaped into the deep forest from colonial-era forced labour and taxes, becoming a wild-people tradition between history and cryptid lore.
appearance: Human figures glimpsed at forest edge, avoiding all contact.
behavior: Shyness is the whole behavior: a people defined by refusal of the state.
deterrents: None; treated as people, not monsters, in the tradition.
popCulture: A rare case where the 'cryptid' has a documented historical kernel.

name: Marapu
origin: The marapu of Sumba: deified ancestors who remain active members of the clan, addressed through megalithic tombs, marapu altars and rato priests — the whole traditional religion of Sumba takes their name.
appearance: Ancestral presence at tombs and clan houses; carved figures house them.
behavior: Govern fertility, law and fortune; neglected marapu withdraw protection.
deterrents: Offerings, ritual speech, tomb feasts — a living religion.
popCulture: Sumba's marapu faith is among Indonesia's most intact ancestral religions.

name: Lulik
origin: Lulik in Timor: the sacred — ancestral spirits, forbidden sacred houses (uma lulik), objects and places charged with ancestral power, approached only under rule and rite.
appearance: Sacred houses and objects; presence rather than figure.
behavior: Taboo enforcement: breach brings illness and misfortune on the whole group.
deterrents: Ritual specialists and strict observance.
popCulture: Uma lulik stand at the centre of Timorese village life.

name: Dewi Anjani
origin: Dewi Anjani, queen of the jinn of Mount Rinjani in Sasak lore, ruler of the spirit court inside the volcano, to whom climbers and the Mulang Pekelem rite at Lake Segara Anak make offerings.
appearance: A regal presence of the crater lake; signs and dreams on the mountain.
behavior: Receives the gold and livestock offerings cast into Segara Anak; storms are her weather.
deterrents: The Mulang Pekelem offering rite; respect on the mountain.
popCulture: Rinjani's spirit court is still honoured by Sasak and Balinese Hindus alike. Variant note (2026-10-22): the Manuk Beri, a spirit bird, belongs to Dewi Anjani’s court in Sasak lore.

name: Putri Mandalika
origin: Princess Mandalika of the Sasak Bau Nyale legend, who threw herself into the sea rather than be fought over by princes, and returns each year as the nyale sea worms gathered in a festival on Lombok's south coast.
appearance: Remembered as the worms themselves and in festival effigy.
behavior: Her annual return is celebrated, not feared — a spirit as calendar.
deterrents: The Bau Nyale festival is the rite.
popCulture: Bau Nyale is one of Lombok's signature living festivals.

name: Ata Polo
origin: Ata polo of Flores: the malevolent sorcerer-being of Nage and neighbouring traditions — a person (or class of being) whose spirit hunts at night, blamed for illness and death, and the Flores cognate of the suanggi complex.
appearance: By day a normal person; by night a hunting spirit presence.
behavior: Nocturnal spiritual predation; accusations historically ended in violence.
deterrents: Counter-ritual and, historically, expulsion — the dataset records the belief, not the practice.
popCulture: Key figure in the ethnography of Flores witchcraft beliefs.

name: Hainuwele
origin: Hainuwele, 'the Coconut Girl' of Seram: the maiden who emerged from a coconut blossom, excreted valuables, and was buried alive by jealous villagers at the Maro dance — from her body grew the food plants. The archipelago's most famous origin myth, recorded by Adolf Jensen.
appearance: A maiden associated with coconut and the moon in the myth.
behavior: Her death originates cultivated plants and, in the myth cycle, mortality itself.
deterrents: None; she is an origin, not a haunting.
popCulture: Central case in comparative mythology since Jensen's Hainuwele (1939).

name: Nunusaku Spirits
origin: The ancestral mother-spirits of Nunusaku, Seram's sacred central mountain — origin place of the Alune and Wemale peoples (Pata Siwa and Pata Lima moieties), whose rivers carry ancestral blessing to the coasts.
appearance: The mountain and its rivers as the ancestors' body.
behavior: Origin and law for Seram's peoples; the mountain is approached under rite.
deterrents: Sacred-site observance.
popCulture: Nunusaku remains the spiritual centre of Seram.

name: Korwar
origin: Korwar of the Biak and Cenderawasih Bay peoples: ancestral spirits housed in carved wooden figures (and historically in prepared skulls), consulted as oracles and guardians — among the most famous ancestral arts of New Guinea.
appearance: Carved standing figures with enlarged heads, once housing the ancestor's skull.
behavior: Oracle and guardian: feasts and consultations keep the ancestor present and favourable.
deterrents: Feast offerings; neglect or theft of a korwar invites ancestral anger.
popCulture: Korwar figures are icons of Papuan art in world museums.

name: Mbis Spirit
origin: The spirits of the Asmat bis (mbis) feast: ancestors invoked and honoured through towering bis poles carved with stacked clan figures, feasted, and then ritually sent on — the ceremonial heart of Asmat life on the Casuarien Coast.
appearance: The bis pole itself: stacked carved ancestors metres tall.
behavior: The feast balances the world of the living and the ancestors (ndat).
deterrents: The feast is the relationship; poles are retired to sago groves to fertilise them.
popCulture: Bis poles are masterpieces of world art, held by the Met and Tropenmuseum.

name: Jiangshi
origin: The jiangshi of Chinese folklore: a stiff reanimated corpse in Qing official dress that hops with arms outstretched, draining qi — the deep outgroup whose hopping locomotion is the classic comparator for the Pocong.
appearance: Stiff corpse in mandarin robes, hopping, arms extended, often with a paper talisman on the forehead.
behavior: Hops toward the living, drawn to breath and qi.
deterrents: Talismans (fulu), glutinous rice, mirrors, holding one's breath.
popCulture: Star of the Hong Kong hopping-vampire film cycle (Mr. Vampire, 1985).

name: Onryo
origin: The onryō of Japan: a soul bound by rage — classically a wronged woman — whose grudge curses places and bloodlines across generations; Sadako and Oiwa are its modern and classical faces, and it is the East Asian pole of the vengeful-female radiation that Kuntilanak anchors in Indonesia.
appearance: White burial kimono, long black hair over the face, limp dangling hands.
behavior: Curse transmission through places, objects and recordings in modern forms.
deterrents: Exorcism rarely works in the tales; the grudge must be answered or outlived.
popCulture: Ring (1998) carried the onryō worldwide.

name: Nat
origin: The 37 Nats of Myanmar: spirits of heroes, ancestors and places, propitiated alongside Buddhism at shrines and nat festivals — the mainland cognate of Indonesia's ancestral-guardian complexes (Datuk Keramat, Tonya, Penunggu).
appearance: Shrine figures in royal dress, possessed mediums (nat kadaw) dancing at festivals.
behavior: Blessing and affliction in the classic guardian pattern.
deterrents: Offerings, festivals, mediums.
popCulture: Nat worship remains woven through Burmese Buddhism.

name: Ma Da
origin: Ma da of Vietnam: the water ghost, spirit of the drowned that must pull a living replacement down to be released — the mainland cognate of Hantu Air and Hantu Banyu, stating the replacement logic explicitly.
appearance: A presence or pale figure dragging swimmers under in rivers and ponds.
behavior: Claims a replacement victim to free itself.
deterrents: Offerings at the water's edge; avoidance of haunted stretches.
popCulture: The replacement-victim logic is shared across mainland and island SE Asia.

name: Pangulubalang
origin: Toba Batak guardian spirit: the bound soul of a boy installed by a datu (priest) into a carved statue or vessel, kept as a village guardian and oracle. Documented in Batak ethnography (Tobing 1956; Warneck; Schuster 1975) and surveyed in a Met Museum collection essay.
appearance: A carved wooden figure or vessel housing the spirit; the being itself is the bound boy-soul within.
behavior: Guards the village, answers the datu's questions, and must be fed and honoured lest it turn restless.
deterrents: It is a kept guardian, not an enemy; neglect is the danger, proper offering the management.
popCulture: Reliefs of pangulubalang stand at the TB Silalahi Center, Balige, on Lake Toba.

name: Geunteut
origin: Acehnese child-abductor as tall as a coconut palm, black and curly-haired, carrying the kanet geunteut, a rice pot that grants endless rice. Studied in Ridwan Hasan's academic paper on Acehnese animism.
appearance: Towering black figure with curly hair, seen at palm groves and village edges.
behavior: Snatches children; in other tellings its stolen rice pot is the prize humans scheme to take.
deterrents: Community vigilance and prayers; the figure is a caution for children near groves at dusk.
popCulture: Recorded across Acehnese folklore collections and university cultural pages (Detak USK).

name: Sowanua (Ono Mbela)
origin: The Sowanua or Ono Mbela of Nias: tree-dwelling first people and forest deity, lord of the wild beasts, from whom hunters must ask permission before hunting. Documented by Hammerle and in Afthonul (2010) and UNIMED journals. The cave-dwelling Nadaoya belong to the same myth cycle (variant note).
appearance: Arboreal human-like people dwelling high in forest trees.
behavior: Rule the forest's animals; grant or withhold hunting luck.
deterrents: Permission-seeking and offerings before hunts — the rite is the relationship.
popCulture: Core being of Nias forest mythology.

name: Taikaleleu
origin: Ruler-spirit of the forest in the Mentawai Arat Sabulungan cosmology, counterpart to Taikamanua of the sky, Taikabaga of the earth and Saikabagakoat of the sea. Documented in a Delfi/Andalas University paper and by anthropologists Sihombing, Delfi and Tulius.
appearance: An unseen sovereign presence of the deep forest of Siberut and the Mentawai islands.
behavior: Governs forest fortune; the kerei (shamans) mediate all dealings with it.
deterrents: Shamanic rite and forest etiquette; not an enemy to be fought.
popCulture: Arat Sabulungan remains a living Mentawai religion.

name: Ketcat Sikatai
origin: Mentawai restless dead: the ketcat sikatai is the spirit of one who died unnaturally (suicide, accident), unable to settle — the dark counterpart of the ketcat simaeru, the blessing-bringing dead. Documented in the Jantro anthropology journal.
appearance: A wandering presence near the place of death.
behavior: Lingers and disturbs until ritual attention settles it.
deterrents: Kerei-led rites to settle the dead.
popCulture: Key category in Mentawai thanatology (Arat Sabulungan).

name: Datuq Jabut
origin: Evil jin of documented Sasak tales from Lombok, with hair so long it sweeps the ground and eyes glowing like a petromax lamp; in the tales the forest-guarding Dewi Anjani hears the weeping it causes. Source: MABASAN journal (Kemendikdasmen).
appearance: A jin figure trailing floor-length hair, eyes burning like pressure-lamp light.
behavior: Haunts forests and frightens travelers in the tale cycle.
deterrents: Religious protection in the tales; Dewi Anjani's court is the counterweight.
popCulture: Published in the Kemendikdasmen language-and-literature journal MABASAN.

name: Balum Beude
origin: Acehnese water demon (also Balum Bili), invisible in rivers and along the coast, which can appear as a floating red rolled mat — the hantu gulung tikar — and drags victims down in whirlpools; in some accounts it takes organs, and it is said to fear gunshots.
appearance: Invisible, or a red mat rolling on the water's surface.
behavior: Creates whirlpools and pulls swimmers under at known stretches.
deterrents: Avoiding its waters; gunfire is said to drive it off in local accounts.
popCulture: Covered by Indonesian cultural outlets (budaya-indonesia.org, Indonesia Sentinel, UNIMAL).

name: Burong Tujoh
origin: The Seven Burong of Aceh: unseen familiar spirits kept by a dukun, sent to possess children and pregnant women, whose victims show red bulging eyes, beast-like behavior and tree-climbing. Distinct from Burong Punjot, the Acehnese Kuntilanak (a variant note, not this taxon). Sources: Correcto news and Sufi et al. as cited in Acehnese folklore writing.
appearance: Unseen; known only by the possessed victim's transformation.
behavior: Possess and torment on their keeper's behalf.
deterrents: Exorcism and confronting the keeper in traditional accounts.
popCulture: Part of recorded Acehnese familiar-spirit lore.

name: Inyiak Harimau
origin: Minangkabau tiger ancestor: the inyiak harimau is a guardian forebear of specific bloodline families who shifts between human and tiger form and protects his descendants — kin in function to the Cindaku of Kerinci but framed as family ancestry. Sources: Minangkabau folklore academic thesis and Holopis.
appearance: A great tiger, or an elder who becomes one.
behavior: Guards the bloodline; appears at family crises and in the forest.
deterrents: A protector: family observance, not deterrence.
popCulture: The tiger-ancestor bond remains a living Minangkabau family tradition.

name: Bicara Guru
origin: Toba Batak family guardian: the begu of a stillborn baby or dead infant, ritually installed as a household guardian spirit with its own shrine and annual feast. Documented in Batak ethnographic writing.
appearance: An infant spirit housed at a small family shrine.
behavior: Watches over the household that feeds and feasts it.
deterrents: Annual feast and offerings maintain the bond.
popCulture: A window into Batak domestic religion (begu taxonomy).

name: Berahu
origin: The named ghost of Nias: a dead person whose required pig-slaughter propitiation rite was skipped, left lingering to disturb their house. Documented in ethnographic text citing Siahaan (1979).
appearance: A presence in its former house.
behavior: Disturbs the household that failed its rites.
deterrents: Performing the skipped pig-slaughter rite settles it.
popCulture: Illustrates how Nias mortuary obligation creates (and resolves) ghosts.

name: Antu Buyu
origin: Iban Dayak witch-spirits: the antu buyu are the bad souls of old women, haunting longhouses, feeding on unswept rice bran and killing newborns. Sources are Sarawak-centric (Sarawak Museum Journal 1983, via KajoMag) — Indonesian Kalimantan Iban share the belief; cross-border sourcing flagged.
appearance: Old-woman spirits about the longhouse at night.
behavior: Feeds on rice-bran leavings; a danger to newborns.
deterrents: Longhouse cleanliness and protective rites.
popCulture: Part of the Iban antu taxonomy recorded by Sarawak Museum ethnography.

name: Lausala
origin: Blood-thirsty spirit of the Gorontalo Polahi tradition, with red eyes and a flaming sword, moving from hill to hill — a barking dog signals its passage. One of the three 'lords' of Polahi lore alongside Pulohuta (land and game) and Lati (tree spirits). Sources: Kompas/Madjowa as cited in Indonesian references and a UNG thesis.
appearance: A figure with burning red eyes carrying a flaming sword.
behavior: Roams the hills at night thirsting for blood.
deterrents: A barking dog is the warning; people stay inside its hours.
popCulture: Completes the Polahi spirit triad alongside the Polahi taxon itself.

name: Dambin-Ow
origin: Asmat evil spirit of a bad or pointless death — dambin-ow — distinct from the good ancestors (yi-ow) and from evil place spirits (osbopan). Documented in Asmat ethnography citing Kal Muller (academia.edu paper). Its corporeality is variable across accounts, coded 0 here.
appearance: A malign presence rather than a fixed body (variable in accounts).
behavior: Afflicts the living from the unresolved manner of its death.
deterrents: Asmat ritual redress of deaths and feuds in traditional practice.
popCulture: Part of the Asmat ow (spirit) taxonomy in the ethnographic record.
